solution:
\(x\,\rho\,y\) holds iff \(x-y\) is zero or irrational.

Reflexive: \(x-x=0\), so \(x\,\rho\,x\) for every real \(x\).

Symmetric: if \(x-y\) is zero or irrational, then so is \(y-x=-(x-y)\).

Not transitive: take \(x=\sqrt2,\ y=0,\ z=\sqrt2-1\). Then \(x-y=\sqrt2\) is irrational, so \(x\,\rho\,y\); and \(y-z=-(\sqrt2-1)=1-\sqrt2\) is irrational, so \(y\,\rho\,z\). But \(x-z=\sqrt2-(\sqrt2-1)=1\), which is rational and non-zero, so \(x\,\rho\,z\) FAILS. Transitivity therefore does not hold.

Hence \(\rho\) is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive. Matches option B.

(Note the shape of the counterexample: two irrational steps whose sum is rational. Choices such as \(1+\sqrt2,\ 1,\ 1-\sqrt2\) do NOT work, since there \(x-z=2\sqrt2\) is still irrational and the relation continues to hold.)
